scenario: AITA for not making my 7 year old brother go to sleep? | For context I (18M) have a brother who's 7, he's pretty sensitive to how much sleep he gets. If he gets less sleep than normal he will be all out of sorts the next day. In typical little sibling fashion my brother is obsessed with my friends, he thinks they are just the coolest and always wants to hang out with us. My friends who don't have little siblings think he's so cute and always hype him up and stuff. Last night my mom left me in charge because she wasn't going to be home until like 1am, and she said it was fine if I had my one friend over because she trusts him. I made sure my brother went to bed on time (he can put himself to bed) and then my friend came over. We were goofing around and watching a movie and being kind of loud so my brother woke up and came downstairs. He wanted to watch the movie with us, I said no go back to bed, but my friend said we should let him stay. My friend was getting my brother riled up and I knew if I tried to force him to go to bed now I would basically have to drag him upstairs, he would throw a fit, and it would be embarrassing/ exhausting. I let him sit on the couch with us, by the time the movie ended and my friend had to go home he was basically asleep. I carried him upstairs (it was like midnight) and put him in bed. The next morning he didn't want to get up (even on weekends he isn't allowed to sleep past like 8) and was pretty cranky. My mom said she knows I let him stay up late and got mad at me. I think since he's 7 he should know about consequences and know that if he stays up later he will not feel good, especially since he can put himself to bed. I also told her 2 hours of missed sleep for a kid his age was not a big deal. AITA for not forcing him to go to bed?

prediction.raw: 1. I think you are not entirely in the wrong for not forcing your brother to go to bed, but your reasoning and approach could be improved. As a 7-year-old, your brother is still developing his self-regulation skills and may not fully understand the consequences of staying up late. While it's great that you want him to learn about responsibility and consequences, it's also important to consider his age and sensitivity to sleep. In this situation, it seems like your friend's influence and the excitement of watching a movie together contributed to your brother's desire to stay up late. Instead of letting him stay up, you could have found alternative solutions, such as setting a specific bedtime or finding a quieter activity to do with your friend. Your argument that 2 hours of missed sleep is not a big deal for a kid his age may not be entirely accurate. While it's true that children can be resilient, consistent sleep patterns are crucial for their physical and emotional development. Disrupting his sleep schedule can have negative effects on his mood, behavior, and overall well-being. It's also important to consider your role as a caregiver and your responsibility to ensure your brother's well-being. As the person in charge, it's your duty to set boundaries and make decisions that prioritize his needs, even if it means disappointing him or your friend. In hindsight, it might have been better to establish clear boundaries and stick to your mom's original instructions. You could have also communicated with your friend about the importance of getting your brother to bed on time and found ways to include him in quieter activities that wouldn't disrupt his sleep schedule. Overall, while your intentions were not entirely wrong, your approach could be improved with more consideration for your brother's needs and well-being.
